stem: A client receiving voriconazole reports new abnormal color perception and photophobia. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: These are recognized voriconazole-associated visual disturbances; if therapy continues beyond 28 days, visual function should be monitored.
options.B: These findings indicate an expected improvement in visual acuity and require no further assessment.
options.C: These findings prove irreversible blindness and require the nurse to tell the client that vision loss will be permanent.
options.D: These findings are unrelated to voriconazole because the medication has no labeled visual adverse effects.

rationale: A is correct. Current DailyMed labeling states that voriconazole-associated visual disturbances are common and can include abnormal vision, color-vision changes, and photophobia. The label also reports prolonged visual adverse reactions such as optic neuritis and papilledema and directs monitoring of visual acuity, visual field, and color perception if treatment continues beyond 28 days. B and D contradict the label. C overstates the prognosis; the label does not say that these symptoms prove permanent blindness, and a controlled 28-day study showed retinal and visual changes returning to normal after therapy ended, while prolonged postmarketing events have also been reported.
educational_objective: Recognize abnormal vision, color-perception changes, and photophobia as labeled voriconazole adverse effects and ensure visual-function monitoring when treatment extends beyond 28 days.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
source_version_date: Current DailyMed label updated May 27, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Warnings and Precautions 5.4 Visual Disturbances: prolonged visual reactions including optic neuritis and papilledema have been reported; if treatment continues beyond 28 days, monitor visual acuity, visual field, and color perception. source_claim_supported: Voriconazole can cause visual disturbances including abnormal/color vision and photophobia; treatment beyond 28 days requires monitoring of visual function, and visual symptoms should not be characterized as uniformly permanent or benign.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw adverse-effect recall item to preserve the current FDA-label nuance: visual effects are recognized and common, prolonged events can occur, and therapy beyond 28 days requires specific visual monitoring. Removed the unsupported blanket claim that the effects are simply transient.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against a current May 2026 DailyMed label, including Warnings 5.4 and the visual-adverse-reaction section.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses the exact symptom and monitoring concepts from the label. B falsely interprets symptoms as benefit. C makes an unsupported universal permanence claim. D denies a labeled adverse effect.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it recognizes the effect and the >28-day monitoring requirement.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; visual changes are adverse effects, not expected improvement.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; symptoms do not prove irreversible blindness.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; the label explicitly describes visual disturbances.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A both identifies the drug relationship and gives the label-supported monitoring implication.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same reported visual symptoms.
audit_findings.blueprint: Adverse-effect recognition and monitoring fit Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked the controlled-study reversibility data against postmarketing prolonged events. The final item avoids saying all events resolve or all are permanent and uses the exact >28-day monitoring threshold from the label. No second answer remained.
